msItem.incipit: Tis no addition to his glorious hearse

abstract.p: This poem is an elegy on the death of John Nycholls, Vicar of Long Ashton. It states that praise in verse can add nothing to him, since his soul is now with the saints, but asks leave to lament the loss. The speaker’s remaining comfort is to say how well he lived and died. His life is described as sermon-like, teaching wholesome doctrine by conduct as well as speech, and as marked by pain yet rich in comfort, so that he became a physician to others, teaching them how to live and die. After his “fiery trial,” the long-wished-for hour of death came, and, dying on a Saturday, he went to keep his Sabbath with the saints in heaven.

div.head:
On Mr John Nycholls Vicar of Longashtonn
Who died upon a Saterday night Dec: 21.
1622

lg.l: ‘Tis no addition to his Glorious herse
To sing His praise, or Ballad out a verse;
No his pure soule (now with the Saintes at praiers)
Lifts him above the Region of such aiers:
Yet give us leave our great losse to lament,
Sorrow would burst us if itt had no vente.
Wee know he’s deade; herin bein blest though,

Since tis some happinesse to
know the worst:
For Hopes and feares only make fortunes thrive,
And with strange art do murther men alive.
All the content now left us is to tell,
How glad wee are hee liv’d and died so well.
To write his life even in the plainest hew
Would seeme Hyperboles, although most trew;
His verie life Was Sermons, and did preach
As wholsome doctrines as his toungue could teach.
And for His life itt ‘twas (my duller braine
Want’s a due attribute) as full of paine as rich in comfort
As rich in Comforte; Comfort did abound,
The helplesse sicke gave cordialls to the sound.
The Patient was Physitian: Who stood by,
By him who taught to live, Were learn’d to dy.
Happy in life and death in end and beirth!
Hee was in Heaven, and yett in Hell on Earth;
For too the hearers comfort hee foorth straines
Most Heavenly raptures in most Hellish paines.
Hee had his fiery triall which being past,
The oft wisht hower of death did come att last:
For having worne out the weeke he went ith Eaven
To keepe his Sabboth with the Saints in Heaven.

div.head: Historical context and dating
div.p: The poem suggests that the speaker knew details of Nichols’s final illness and death, referring to the “fiery triall” of his last sickness and stating that he died on a Saturday night, implying a close association between writer and subject. Nichols as ordained priest on 20 September 1607 and as Vicar of Long Ashton from July 1618 until October 1623, the latter date likely marking the refilling of the benefice rather than the exact date of his death (Clergy of the Church of England Database). The manuscript context supports a local connection: as noted in the Folger catalog Folger catalog, the volume belonged to the Smith (Smithe/Smyth) family of Long Ashton, Somerset, whose names—John, Hugh, and Charles—appear in the book between 1674 and 1690, suggesting a personal or familial link between the manuscript’s owners and the subject of the poem.
